sn35.92:2.2: The same “duality” is described as the (sentient) body and “external” name and form, which are essential for contact through the six senses ([sn12.19:1.3]()). This recalls the ‘duality” spoken of by Yājñavalkya as his culminating philosophy: “For when there is a duality, as it were, then one smells the other, one sees the other, one hears the other, one greets the other, one thinks of the other, one cognizes the other. By what would one cognize that which cognizes this All? By what would one cognize the cognizer?” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). It is not obvious how the “duality” of existence and nonexistence can be reconciled with the claim here ([sn22.90:9.2]()).
